chunks.text:
A set is a collection of distinct objects, called its _elements_ or _members_.

Set theory studies which axiom systems make this idea behave; the working axiom system is [ZFC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zermelo–Fraenkel_set_theory).

The field began with Cantor's work on ::infinite cardinalities{h4}::.

[Russell's paradox](/thoughts/Wittgenstein#russell-s-paradox-and-the-vicious-circle-principle) is the canonical obstruction you hit when first studying naive set theory: the set $R = \{x \mid x \notin x\}$ would satisfy $R \in R \iff R \notin R$.

[ZFC](/thoughts/Sets#zermelo-fraenkel-set-theory) addresses this via comprehension, where the axiom of separation only lets you carve a subset $\{x \in A \mid \dots\}$ out of an existing set $A$, so the unrestricted $R$ is never formed. <small>(The axiom of foundation additionally forbids $x \in x$ chains.)</small>

Sets are the substrate for [algebraic structures](/thoughts/algebraic-geometry) and the mathematical spaces studied in #math/topology.

## notation

| symbol           | meaning                                                                   |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| $x \in A$        | $x$ is an element of $A$                                                  |
| $x \not\in A$    | $x$ is not an element of $A$                                              |
| $A \subseteq B$  | every element of $A$ is in $B$                                            |
| $A \subsetneq B$ | $A$ is a _proper subset_ of $B$: $A \subseteq B$ and $A \neq B$           |
| $A \cup B$       | [union](/thoughts/Sets#a-cup-b): $\{x \mid x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}$         |
| $A \cap B$       | [intersection](/thoughts/Sets#a-cap-b): $\{x \mid x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}$ |
| $A \setminus B$  | [difference](/thoughts/Sets#difference): $\{x \in A \mid x \notin B\}$                |
| $\emptyset$      | [empty set](/thoughts/Sets#empty)                                                     |
| $\mathcal{P}(A)$ | [power set](/thoughts/Sets#power-set): all subsets of $A$                             |
| $A \times B$     | [Cartesian products](/thoughts/Sets#cartesian-products)                               |
| $\neg P$         | negation                                                                  |

> [!note] inclusion
>
> $\subseteq$ and $\subsetneq$ are _inclusion_ and _proper inclusion_ respectively
>
> We can also express the notion that "$A$ and $B$ have no common items <small>(We can also say that $A$ and $B$ are disjoint.)</small>" via the empty set, or $A \cap B = \emptyset$

## set-builder notation

The [set-builder notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set-builder_notation) expression <small>(this is domain-bound format, which is safe.)</small> $\{x \in A \mid P(x)\}$ means _start with an existing set $A$, then keep exactly the elements satisfying $P$_.

$$
\{x \in A \mid P(x)\} \subseteq A
$$

> naive form $\{x \mid P(x)\}$ _assumes that every predicate determines a set, where Russell's paradox would then choose_ $P(x)$ _to be_ $x \notin x$

ZFC addresses this via separation:

$$
\forall\;A\;\exists\;B\;\forall x\;(x \in B \iff x \in A \land P(x))
$$

> [!axiom] extensionality
>
> Sets are determined by their elements:
>
> $$
> \forall\;A\;\forall\;B\;(\forall x\;(x \in A \iff x \in B) \implies A = B)
> $$
>
> Order and repetition ::do not matter:: when we consider members of a set. <small>(We will consider surjective, bijective, and [injective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bijection,_injection_and_surjection#Injection) properties of sets [below](/thoughts/Sets#surjection-bijection-injection).)</small>
>
> $$
> \{1,2,3\} = \{3,2,1,1\}\;\; \text{ (axiom of extensionality)}
> $$

### empty

_the set with no elements_, also see [Russell's paradox](/thoughts/Wittgenstein#russell-s-paradox-and-the-vicious-circle-principle)

for union and intersection we can define

$$
\begin{aligned}
  A \cup \emptyset &= A \\
  A \cap \emptyset &= \emptyset
\end{aligned}
$$

```lean shell
import Mathlib

theorem union_empty {α : Type*} (A : Set α) : A ∪ ∅ = A := by
  apply Set.ext
  intro x
  exact ⟨fun h => Or.elim h id False.elim, Or.inl⟩

theorem inter_empty {α : Type*} (A : Set α) : A ∩ ∅ = ∅ := by
  apply Set.ext
  intro x
  exact ⟨fun ⟨_, h⟩ => h, False.elim⟩

#check @union_empty
#check @inter_empty
```

### contrapositive and converse

"if...then" would often concern relation between _statement_, _contrapositive_ or _converse_

| logic           | notation                                   |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| If $P$ then $Q$ | $P \implies Q$                             |
| contrapositive  | $(\text{not } Q) \implies (\text{not } P)$ |
| converse        | $Q \implies P$                             |

> A statement and its contrapositive are _logically equivalent_. The converse can have a different truth value.
>
> If the converse also holds, then $P \iff Q$.

The universal and existential quantifiers are the grammar behind most set statements:

| logic                         | notation           |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------ |
| for all elements              | $\forall x \in A$  |
| there exists an element       | $\exists x \in A$  |
| there exists a unique element | $\exists!x \in A$  |
| no element exists             | $\nexists x \in A$ |

Negation flips quantifiers:

$$
\neg(\forall x \in A,\;P(x)) \iff \exists x \in A,\;\neg P(x)
$$

$$
\neg(\exists x \in A,\;P(x)) \iff \forall x \in A,\;\neg P(x)
$$

```lean shell
import Mathlib

theorem contrapositive_iff (P Q : Prop) : (P → Q) ↔ (¬ Q → ¬ P) := by
  constructor
  · intro hpq hnq hp
    exact hnq (hpq hp)
  · intro hcontra hp
    exact Classical.byContradiction (fun hnq => hcontra hnq hp)

theorem not_exists_mem_iff {α : Type*} (A : Set α) (P : α → Prop) :
    ¬ (∃ x, x ∈ A ∧ P x) ↔ ∀ x, x ∈ A → ¬ P x := by
  constructor
  · intro hne x hxa hpx
    exact hne ⟨x, hxa, hpx⟩
  · intro hall ⟨x, hxa, hpx⟩
    exact hall x hxa hpx

#check @contrapositive_iff
#check @not_exists_mem_iff
```

## set operations

We can visualize the basic operations and rules of set theory via Venn diagrams

### ($A \cup B$)

The union contains all elements that are in $A$, or in $B$, or in both.

<small>diagram</small>

### ($A \cap B$)

The intersection contains all elements that are in both $A$ and $B$.

<small>diagram</small>

### ($A \setminus B$)

The difference (or relative complement) contains all elements that are in $A$ but not in $B$.

It is also known as the _complement_ of $B$ relative to $A$, or the complement of $B$ in $A$.

<small>diagram</small>

### distributive

For sets $A,B,C$:

$$A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$$

<small>diagram</small>

> [!note] order of operations
>

> Union and intersection are each commutative and associative. This example mixes the two operations, so the parentheses change the result. In general,
>
> $$
> A \cup (B \cap C) \neq (A \cup B) \cap C.
> $$
>
> The distributive law is
>
> $$
> A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C).
> $$
>
> $A \cup (B \cap C)$ and $(A \cup B) \cap C$:
>
> <small>diagram</small>

```lean shell
import Mathlib

theorem inter_distrib_left {α : Type*} (A B C : Set α) :
    A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) := by
  apply Set.ext
  intro x
  exact ⟨
    fun ⟨ha, hbc⟩ => Or.elim hbc (fun hb => Or.inl ⟨ha, hb⟩) (fun hc => Or.inr ⟨ha, hc⟩),
    fun h => Or.elim h (fun ⟨ha, hb⟩ => ⟨ha, Or.inl hb⟩) (fun ⟨ha, hc⟩ => ⟨ha, Or.inr hc⟩)
  ⟩

theorem union_distrib_left {α : Type*} (A B C : Set α) :
    A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C) := by
  apply Set.ext
  intro x
  exact ⟨
    fun h => Or.elim h (fun ha => ⟨Or.inl ha, Or.inl ha⟩) (fun ⟨hb, hc⟩ => ⟨Or.inr hb, Or.inr hc⟩),
    fun ⟨hab, hac⟩ => Or.elim hab Or.inl (fun hb => Or.elim hac Or.inl (fun hc => Or.inr ⟨hb, hc⟩))
  ⟩

#check @inter_distrib_left
#check @union_distrib_left
```

### de Morgan's laws

For sets $A,B,C$:

$$
A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C)
$$

<small>diagram</small>

$$
A \setminus (B\cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)
$$

<small>diagram</small>

> [!important] de Morgan's laws verbatim
>

> _The complement of the union equals the intersection of the complements_
>
> _The complement of the intersection equals the union of the complements_
>
> ```lean shell
> import Mathlib
>
> theorem de_morgan_diff_union {α : Type*} (A B C : Set α) :
>     A \ (B ∪ C) = (A \ B) ∩ (A \ C) := by
>   apply Set.ext
>   intro x
>   simp only [Set.mem_diff, Set.mem_union, Set.mem_inter_iff]
>   exact ⟨
>     fun ⟨ha, hbc⟩ => ⟨⟨ha, fun hb => hbc (Or.inl hb)⟩, ⟨ha, fun hc => hbc (Or.inr hc)⟩⟩,
>     fun ⟨⟨ha, hnb⟩, ⟨_, hnc⟩⟩ => ⟨ha, fun hbc => Or.elim hbc hnb hnc⟩
>   ⟩
>
> theorem de_morgan_diff_inter {α : Type*} (A B C : Set α) :
>     A \ (B ∩ C) = (A \ B) ∪ (A \ C) := by
>   apply Set.ext
>   intro x
>   constructor
>   · intro ⟨ha, hnbc⟩
>     exact Or.elim (Classical.em (x ∈ B))
>       (fun hb => Or.inr ⟨ha, fun hc => hnbc ⟨hb, hc⟩⟩)
>       (fun hnb => Or.inl ⟨ha, hnb⟩)
>   · intro h
>     exact Or.elim h
>       (fun ⟨ha, hnb⟩ => ⟨ha, fun ⟨hb, _⟩ => hnb hb⟩)
>       (fun ⟨ha, hnc⟩ => ⟨ha, fun ⟨_, hc⟩ => hnc hc⟩)
>
> #check @de_morgan_diff_union
> #check @de_morgan_diff_inter
> ```

### sets algebra

For a fixed universe $X$, we write $A^c = X \setminus A$.

| law               | union form                              | intersection form                       |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| identity          | $A \cup \emptyset = A$                  | $A \cap X = A$                          |
| domination        | $A \cup X = X$                          | $A \cap \emptyset = \emptyset$          |
| idempotent        | $A \cup A = A$                          | $A \cap A = A$                          |
| commutative       | $A \cup B = B \cup A$                   | $A \cap B = B \cap A$                   |
| associative       | $(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)$ | $(A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C)$ |
| absorption        | $A \cup (A \cap B) = A$                 | $A \cap (A \cup B) = A$                 |
| complement        | $A \cup A^c = X$                        | $A \cap A^c = \emptyset$                |
| double complement | $(A^c)^c = A$                           | $(X \setminus A)^c = A$                 |

Set difference is intersection with a complement:

$$
A \setminus B = A \cap B^c
$$

> [!proof] set difference
>
> For arbitrary $x \in X$,
>
> $$
> \begin{aligned}
>   x \in A \setminus B
>     &\iff x \in A \land x \notin B \\
>     &\iff x \in A \land x \in B^c \\
>     &\iff x \in A \cap B^c
> \end{aligned}
> $$
>
> Hence $A \setminus B$ and $A \cap B^c$ have the same elements. By extensionality,
>
> $$
> A \setminus B = A \cap B^c.
> $$
>
> ```lean shell
> import Mathlib
>
> theorem set_diff_eq_inter_compl {α : Type*} (A B : Set α) : A \ B = A ∩ Bᶜ := by
>   ext x
>   rfl
>
> #check @set_diff_eq_inter_compl
> ```

The symmetric difference keeps elements that appear in exactly one set:

$$
A\triangle B = (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A)
$$

Equivalently, membership in $A \triangle B$ is exclusive-or:

$$
x \in A\triangle B \iff (x \in A \land x \notin B) \lor (x \notin A \land x \in B)
$$

```lean shell
import Mathlib

def setSymmDiff {α : Type*} (A B : Set α) : Set α := (A \ B) ∪ (B \ A)

theorem setSymmDiff_comm {α : Type*} (A B : Set α) :
    setSymmDiff A B = setSymmDiff B A := by
  apply Set.ext
  intro x
  exact ⟨fun h => Or.elim h Or.inr Or.inl, fun h => Or.elim h Or.inr Or.inl⟩

theorem setSymmDiff_self {α : Type*} (A : Set α) :
    setSymmDiff A A = ∅ := by
  apply Set.ext
  intro x
  exact ⟨fun h => Or.elim h (fun ⟨ha, hna⟩ => hna ha) (fun ⟨ha, hna⟩ => hna ha), False.elim⟩

#check @setSymmDiff_comm
#check @setSymmDiff_self
```

### power set

> [!important] correct notation
>
> a distinction between object $a$, which is an _element of the set_ $A$, and one-element set $\{a\}$, which is a _subset of_ $A$
>
> If $A$ is the set $\{a, b, c\}$ then
>
> $a \in A,\;\;\;\;\{a\} \subseteq A,\;\;\;\; \{a\} \in \mathcal{P}(A)$

The clean model is a subset as its characteristic function:

$$
S \subseteq A \quad\leftrightarrow\quad \chi_S: A \to \{0,1\}
$$

where $\chi_S(x)=1$ exactly when $x \in S$. Thus $\mathcal{P}(A)$ bijects with $\{0,1\}^A$, the set of all functions from $A$ to $\{0,1\}$.

For $A = \{a,b,c\}$, fix the coordinate order $(a,b,c)$. A subset is then a length-$3$ bit-vector:

$$
\{a,c\} \leftrightarrow 101
$$

Thus $\mathcal{P}(A)$ bijects with $\{0,1\}^3$:

$$
\mathcal{P}(\{a,b,c\}) \cong \{0,1\}^3
$$

If $A$ has $n$ elements, then each subset of $A$ is one binary string in $\{0,1\}^n$. Each coordinate answers one membership question, so $n$ yes/no questions give $2^n$ subsets.

> [!theorem] Cantor's theorem
>
> For every set $A$, there is no surjection $f: A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$.
>
> Proof:
>
> Assume a surjection $f$ exists, and form the diagonal set
>
> $$
> D = \{a \in A \mid a \notin f(a)\}.
> $$
>
> Since $f$ is surjective, $D = f(d)$ for some $d \in A$. Then $d \in D \iff d \notin f(d) \iff d \notin D$, contradiction.
>
> Therefore $\mathcal{P}(A)$ has strictly larger cardinality than $A$.
>
> ```lean shell
> import Mathlib
>
> theorem cantor_diagonal {α : Type*} (f : α → Set α) : ¬ Function.Surjective f := by
>   intro hsurj
>   let D : Set α := {a | a ∉ f a}
>   obtain ⟨d, hd⟩ := hsurj D
>   have hiff : d ∈ f d ↔ d ∉ f d := by
>     conv => lhs; rw [hd]
>     rfl
>   exact (iff_not_self hiff)
>
> #check @cantor_diagonal
> ```

### arbitrary unions and intersection

_union of the elements of_ $\mathcal{A}$ is defined by

$$
\bigcup_{A \in \mathcal{A}}\; A = \{x \mid x \in A \text{ for at least one } A \in \mathcal{A}\}
$$

_intersection of the elements of_ $\mathcal{A}$ is defined by

$$
\bigcap_{A \in \mathcal{A}}\; A = \{x \mid x \in A \text{ for every } A \in \mathcal{A}\}
$$

> [!important] universality of $\emptyset$
> If $\emptyset \in \mathcal{A}$, the union is not forced to be empty. The empty set contributes no elements, then the other members still contribute theirs.
>
> If $\mathcal{A} = \emptyset$, then $\bigcup_{A \in \mathcal{A}} A = \emptyset$.
>
> If $\mathcal{A} = \emptyset$ and we are working inside a universe $X$, then every $x \in X$ vacuously satisfies the defining property for intersection, so
>
> $$
> \bigcap_{A \in \emptyset} A = X
> $$

An _indexed family_ of sets is a function $I \to \mathcal{P}(X)$, usually written $\{A_i\}_{i \in I}$ instead of $i \mapsto A_i$.

$$
\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \{x \in X \mid \exists i \in I,\;x \in A_i\}
$$

$$
\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \{x \in X \mid \forall i \in I,\;x \in A_i\}
$$

The index set $I$ is bookkeeping; the sets $A_i$ are the mathematical objects. Different indices may name the same subset.

```lean shell
import Mathlib

theorem compl_iUnion {α : Type*} {ι : Type*} (A : ι → Set α) :
    (⋃ i, A i)ᶜ = ⋂ i, (A i)ᶜ := by
  ext x
  simp

#check @compl_iUnion
```

> [!note]+ repetition value within a family
>
> A family can have repeated values because it is a function out of $I$. A set cannot have repeated elements because extensionality deletes repetitions.

### Cartesian products

_notion of ordered pair_ over to general sets. We define a _Cartesian product_ $A \times B$ to be the set of all ordered pairs $(a,b)$ for which $a$ is an element of $A$ and $b$ is an element of $B$.

$$
A \times B = \{(a,b) \mid\;a \in A \text{ and } b \in B\}
$$

> Kuratowski defines $(a,b)$ as $\{\{a\}, \{a,b\}\}$. The singleton marks the first coordinate. If $a=b$, the pair collapses to $\{\{a\}\}$, which still recovers $(a,a)$.

## relations

A binary relation from $A$ to $B$ is a subset $R \subseteq A \times B$. If $(a,b) \in R$, write $aRb$.

On a set $A$, a relation $R \subseteq A \times A$ can have extra structure:

| property      | meaning                            |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| reflexive     | $\forall a \in A,\;aRa$            |
| symmetric     | $aRb \implies bRa$                 |
| antisymmetric | $(aRb \land bRa) \implies a = b$   |
| transitive    | $(aRb \land bRc) \implies aRc$     |
| total         | $\forall a,b \in A,\;aRb \lor bRa$ |

An _equivalence relation_ is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. It partitions $A$ into equivalence classes:

$$
[a] = \{x \in A \mid x \sim a\}
$$

The quotient set $A/{\sim}$ is the set of all equivalence classes.

```lean shell
import Mathlib

theorem equiv_class_eq_iff {α : Type*} {r : α → α → Prop} (heq : Equivalence r) (a b : α) :
    r a b ↔ ({x : α | r x a} : Set α) = {x : α | r x b} := by
  constructor
  · intro hab
    apply Set.ext
    intro x
    exact ⟨fun hxa => heq.trans hxa hab, fun hxb => heq.trans hxb (heq.symm hab)⟩
  · intro hset
    have haa : a ∈ ({x : α | r x a} : Set α) := heq.refl a
    rw [hset] at haa
    exact haa

#check @equiv_class_eq_iff
```

A _partial order_ is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.

A _total order_ is a partial order where any two elements are comparable.

## functions

> [!math] rule of assignment
>
> A relation $r \subseteq C \times D$ is a partial function from $C$ to $D$ when each $c \in C$ is paired with at most one $d \in D$:
>
> $$
> \forall c \in C\;\forall d,d' \in D,\quad ((c,d) \in r \land (c,d') \in r) \implies d=d'.
> $$
>
> It is total when every $c \in C$ is paired with exactly one $d \in D$.

A function $f: A \to B$ is a total relation $f \subseteq A \times B$:

$$
\forall a \in A\;\exists! b \in B\;(a,b) \in f
$$

The ::domain:: is $A$, the codomain is $B$, and the image is

$$
f(A) = \{b \in B \mid \exists a \in A,\;f(a)=b\}
$$

For $S,U \subseteq A$ and $T,V \subseteq B$:

$$
f(S) = \{f(s) \mid s \in S\}
$$

$$
f^{-1}(T) = \{a \in A \mid f(a) \in T\}
$$

[Preimages](/thoughts/preimages) preserve the Boolean operations exactly:

$$
f^{-1}(T \cup V) = f^{-1}(T) \cup f^{-1}(V)
$$

$$
f^{-1}(T \cap V) = f^{-1}(T) \cap f^{-1}(V)
$$

$$
f^{-1}(B \setminus T) = A \setminus f^{-1}(T)
$$

Images preserve unions:

$$
f(S \cup U) = f(S) \cup f(U)
$$

Images only preserve intersections one way in general:

$$
f(S \cap U) \subseteq f(S) \cap f(U)
$$

```lean shell
import Mathlib

theorem preimage_union {α β : Type*} (f : α → β) (T V : Set β) :
    f ⁻¹' (T ∪ V) = f ⁻¹' T ∪ f ⁻¹' V := by
  apply Set.ext
  intro x
  rfl

theorem image_inter_subset {α β : Type*} (f : α → β) (S U : Set α) :
    f '' (S ∩ U) ⊆ f '' S ∩ f '' U := by
  intro y hy
  obtain ⟨x, ⟨hxs, hxu⟩, rfl⟩ := hy
  exact ⟨⟨x, hxs, rfl⟩, ⟨x, hxu, rfl⟩⟩

#check @preimage_union
#check @image_inter_subset
```

### surjection, bijection, injection

Equality holds when $f$ is injective.

```lean shell
import Mathlib

theorem image_inter_eq_of_injective {α β : Type*} {f : α → β}
    (hinj : Function.Injective f) (S U : Set α) :
    f '' (S ∩ U) = f '' S ∩ f '' U := by
  apply Set.ext
  intro y
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨x, ⟨hxs, hxu⟩, rfl⟩
    exact ⟨⟨x, hxs, rfl⟩, ⟨x, hxu, rfl⟩⟩
  · rintro ⟨⟨x₁, hx₁, rfl⟩, ⟨x₂, hx₂, heq⟩⟩
    have hx : x₂ = x₁ := hinj heq
    exact ⟨x₁, ⟨hx₁, hx ▸ hx₂⟩, rfl⟩

theorem bijective_comp {α β γ : Type*} {g : β → γ} {f : α → β}
    (hg : Function.Bijective g) (hf : Function.Bijective f) :
    Function.Bijective (fun x => g (f x)) := by
  refine ⟨fun a b h => hf.1 (hg.1 h), fun c => ?_⟩
  obtain ⟨b, rfl⟩ := hg.2 c
  obtain ⟨a, rfl⟩ := hf.2 b
  exact ⟨a, rfl⟩

#check @image_inter_eq_of_injective
#check @bijective_comp
```

| type       | condition                                   |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| injective  | $f(a)=f(a') \implies a=a'$                  |
| surjective | $\forall b \in B\;\exists a \in A,\;f(a)=b$ |
| bijective  | injective and surjective                    |
<small>diagram</small>

## cardinality

Two sets have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection between them:

$$
|A| = |B| \iff \exists f: A \to B \text{ bijective}
$$

For finite sets:

$$
|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|
$$

For finite products:

$$
|A \times B| = |A||B|
$$

A set is _countably infinite_ if it bijects with $\mathbb{N}$. The integers and rationals are countable; the reals are uncountable.

> [!math] diagonal argument
>
> The set $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ of infinite binary sequences is _uncountable_.
>
> If a list claimed to contain every such sequence, construct a new sequence $b$ by setting $b_n = 1 - a_{n,n}$ <small>(where $a_{n,n}$ is the $n$th bit of the $n$th listed sequence)</small>. Then $b$ differs from row $n$ at bit $n$, so it is missing from the list.

## open

A _topology_ on a set $X$ is a collection $\tau \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ whose members are called _open sets_, satisfying (munkres §12):

- $\emptyset, X \in \tau$
- arbitrary unions of open sets are open
- finite intersections of open sets are open

The pair $(X, \tau)$ is a _topological space_. The same $X$ can carry many topologies: the discrete topology ($\tau = \mathcal{P}(X)$), the indiscrete topology ($\tau = \{\emptyset, X\}$), and any topology in between.

For $X = \mathbb{R}$ with the standard topology, $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open iff every $x \in U$ has some $\varepsilon > 0$ with $(x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon) \subseteq U$.

## closed

A set $C \subseteq X$ is _closed_ if its complement $X \setminus C$ is open. Equivalently (munkres §17):

- $\emptyset, X$ are closed
- arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed
- finite unions of closed sets are closed

Closed and open are not exclusive. In the discrete topology every set is both. In $\mathbb{R}$ with the standard topology, $[a, b]$ is closed, $(a, b)$ is open, and $[a, b)$ is neither. The half-open structure is what makes the lower limit topology distinct from the standard one.

The _closure_ $\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed set containing $A$; the _interior_ $\mathrm{int}(A)$ is the largest open set inside $A$. Their difference $\overline{A} \setminus \mathrm{int}(A)$ is the boundary $\partial A$.

Open and closed are properties of subsets relative to a topology on $X$, not absolute properties of the raw set.

The Lean structure below keeps the assumptions needed to prove that a union of two closed sets is closed. It omits closure under arbitrary unions of open sets, so its `Topology` name describes a weaker structure than the topology defined above. Mathlib's [`TopologicalSpace`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Topology/Defs/Basic.html#TopologicalSpace) includes that missing axiom. The proof here uses only complements and the intersection axiom.

```lean shell
import Mathlib

structure Topology (α : Type*) where
  IsOpen : Set α → Prop
  isOpen_empty : IsOpen ∅
  isOpen_univ : IsOpen Set.univ
  isOpen_inter : ∀ ⦃U V : Set α⦄, IsOpen U → IsOpen V → IsOpen (U ∩ V)

def Topology.IsClosed {α : Type*} (τ : Topology α) (C : Set α) : Prop :=
  τ.IsOpen Cᶜ

theorem Topology.isClosed_union {α : Type*} (τ : Topology α) {C D : Set α}
    (hC : τ.IsClosed C) (hD : τ.IsClosed D) :
    τ.IsClosed (C ∪ D) := by
  unfold Topology.IsClosed at *
  have hcompl : (C ∪ D)ᶜ = Cᶜ ∩ Dᶜ := by
    apply Set.ext
    intro x
    exact ⟨fun h => ⟨fun hc => h (Or.inl hc), fun hd => h (Or.inr hd)⟩,
           fun ⟨hnc, hnd⟩ h => Or.elim h hnc hnd⟩
  rw [hcompl]
  exact τ.isOpen_inter hC hD

#check @Topology.isClosed_union
```

## Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory

ZFC is an [axiomatic system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiomatic_system) that was proposed to formulate a paradox-free theory of sets to address [Russell's paradox](/thoughts/Wittgenstein#russell-s-paradox-and-the-vicious-circle-principle). Formally, it is intended to formalize a single primitive notion, that of a [hereditary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hereditary_set) [well-founded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well-founded_relation) set, so that all _entities_ in the universe of discourse are sets.

> These axioms of ZFC therefore refer only to [pure sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hereditary_set) and prevent its models from containing urelements <small>(elements that are not themselves sets.)</small>

Formally, ZFC is a one-sorted theory in [first-order logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-order_logic).

The only nonlogical primitive is membership $\in$. Equality is governed by extensionality, and every other construction gets encoded through sets.

| axiom              | job                                                                    |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| extensionality     | same elements means same set                                           |
| empty set          | there exists a set with no elements                                    |
| pairing            | from $a,b$, form $\{a,b\}$                                             |
| union              | from a set of sets, form the set of their members                      |
| power set          | from $A$, form $\mathcal{P}(A)$                                        |
| infinity           | there exists an inductive set, giving enough material for $\mathbb{N}$ |
| separation schema  | carve subsets from existing sets by first-order predicates             |
| replacement schema | images of sets under definable functions are sets                      |
| foundation         | rules out infinite descending membership chains                        |
| choice             | for a set of nonempty sets, choose one element from each               |

Replacement is stronger than Separation.

- Separation says "filter this set."
- Replacement says "send each element through a definable rule, then collect the outputs."

> [!note] universality
> Complements need a universe. $A^c$ means $X \setminus A$ only after $X$ has been fixed.

$$
\forall x \in A\;\exists!y\;\varphi(x,y) \implies \exists B\;\forall y\;(y \in B \iff \exists x \in A\;\varphi(x,y))
$$

The axiom of choice has many equivalent forms:

- every surjection has a right inverse
- every vector space has a basis
- every product of nonempty sets is nonempty
- every set can be well-ordered
